title: Quality Management
sequence: Planning (requirements and the plan); quality assurance then runs through Executing, quality control through Monitoring & Controlling, with reviews and improvement throughout.

header.html: Process domain (41%) · Task 7 Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables — gather quality requirements for project deliverables · plan quality processes and tools · execute a quality management plan · help ensure regulatory compliance · manage cost of quality (CoQ) and sustainability · conduct ongoing quality reviews · implement continuous improvement

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Quality The degree to which the inherent characteristics of a deliverable help meet or exceed the project's target objectives
Quality management plan Describes how the organization's policies, procedures and guidelines will be implemented to reach the quality objectives. Formal or informal, detailed or broad; review it early so decisions use accurate information (sharper focus on value, lower cost, fewer overruns caused by rework)
Quality assurance (QA) Using project processes effectively and following standards, to assure stakeholders the results will meet needs. Related ideas: regulations, compliance, audits
Quality control (QC) Creating deliverables that meet defined specifications and thresholds: defining the attributes of the value generated and ensuring deliverables achieve them. Related ideas: product design, testing, defects
Quality metric Describes a project or product attribute and how QA will verify compliance with it. Examples: % tasks completed on time, CPI, failure rates, defects found per day, downtime per month, errors per line of code, customer satisfaction scores, test coverage (% of requirements covered by tests)
Specification / tolerance Specification: an attribute that must be present in a deliverable. Tolerance: the quantified acceptable variation for a requirement
Conformance / nonconformance Conformance: the degree to which results meet the quality requirements; nonconformance is the failure to do so
Rework / defect repair Action to bring a defective or nonconforming component into compliance
Control limits vs specification limits Control limits are calculated from the process's own data with standard statistical methods (usually ±3 standard deviations Beyond PMBOK 8number); specification limits come from the requirements. They are different (section 6)
Verification / validation Verification: complies with requirement or specification. Validation: meets the customer's and stakeholders' needs (Topic 15)
Definition of done (DoD) / definition of ready DoD: criteria for work to count as complete (include tests, documentation and compliance). Definition of ready ("full kit"): a checklist confirming work is ready to start, which minimizes rework
Cost of quality (CoQ) All costs of preventing, appraising and failing to meet requirements (section 9)
Grade vs quality Beyond PMBOK 8 Grade is a category with the same function but different features (basic vs deluxe): low grade is not a problem, low quality is
Precision vs accuracy Beyond PMBOK 8 Precision: repeated measurements cluster together. Accuracy: measurements are close to the true value. A process can be one without the other
Prevention over inspection Beyond PMBOK 8phrasing Quality is planned in, not inspected in; preventing a defect costs less than finding it, and finding it early costs less than finding it late

2Quality Across the Project

Quality assurance Quality control
Focus The processes and standards The deliverables and their specifications
Nature Preventive; builds confidence future output will conform Detective; finds nonconformance so it can be repaired
Typical tools Audits, checklists, process analysis, root cause analysis, process improvement, cause-and-effect and flow diagrams Inspections, testing, control charts, variance and trend analysis, histograms, sampling
PMBOK 8 home Governance domain: Manage Quality Assurance Scope domain: Monitor and Control Scope
Key outputs Quality reports, change requests Verified deliverables, quality control measurements, quality reports, change requests
Who The project management team, an external entity, or both The team and quality function
Formality Predictive: usually formal. Adaptive: formal or informal as the context needs Continuous; in agile work built into each iteration's DoD

After control, Validate Scope checks the processes used to reach the quality standards and obtains customer acceptance (Topic 15). Memory aid: audit a process (QA); inspect or test a product (QC).

3Gather Quality Requirements (ECO)

Where they come from: stakeholder expectations and needs, the business case and success criteria, contracts, regulations and standards (EEFs and OPAs), organizational policies, product attributes (performance, reliability, safety, security, usability and other functional and nonfunctional requirements).

Practice Notes
Capture them as requirements PMBOK 8 classifies quality requirements as conditions or criteria needed to validate completion: tests, certifications, validations. Record them in requirements documentation and the RTM
Make them measurable and testable Acceptance criteria, metrics and thresholds; vague goals ("high quality") need measurable outcomes
Identify them in Define Scope The scope domain identifies quality requirements and standards and how compliance will be demonstrated (Topic 15)
Techniques Interviews, focus groups, surveys, benchmarking, document analysis (regulations, standards), customer talks and tests, prototypes, observation
Compliance and sustainability Regulatory requirements and customer-required sustainability criteria (for example water-use certification) are quality requirements; manage them inside the quality plan and controls
Agile Acceptance criteria on each story plus a definition of done that includes testing, documentation and compliance; update criteria as the product evolves

4Plan Quality Processes and Tools (ECO)

The quality management plan may include:

Component Content
Quality standards Standards the project will use (organizational, industry, regulatory)
Quality objectives What the project must achieve
Roles and responsibilities Who plans, assures, controls, audits
Deliverables and processes subject to quality review What is reviewed, when and by whom
QC and QA activities Planned reviews, audits, tests, inspections
Tools and methodologies Checklists, charts, sampling, testing methods
Nonconformance and continuous improvement Procedures for handling defects and for improving

Plan these items:

  • Quality metrics and the way QA will verify them (and the format of QC measurements).
  • Test and inspection planning: how each product or deliverable will be tested or inspected to meet stakeholder needs and performance and reliability goals. Tests are industry dependent: software (unit, integration, black-box, white-box, interface, regression, alpha), construction (concrete strength and workability, nondestructive tests, soil tests), hardware (environmental stress screening, burn-in, system tests).
  • How compliance will be verified, not only which specifications apply. Specifications without verification methods leave a gap.
  • Quality activities in the schedule, budget and resources (cost of quality; Topics 16, 17, 19); do quality work as early as possible ("shift left").
  • Prevention first: training, documented processes, definition of ready, checklists, reviews of the quality plan.
  • Tailor the plan (section 11).

5Execute the Plan: Manage Quality Assurance

Purpose (PMBOK 8): ensure project processes are performed consistently with stakeholder expectations by turning the plan into executable activities that include organizational standards, regulations and policies. Benefits: confidence that output will meet requirements (through audits and failure analysis); better efficiency and effectiveness of processes; proper governance, and a higher chance of meeting or exceeding expectations. It also identifies ineffective processes and the causes of poor performance. It runs throughout the project.

Tool Use
Quality audit A structured, independent process to determine whether activities comply with organizational and project policies and procedures. Usually by a team outside the project (internal audit, PMO or an external auditor); scheduled or random. Objectives: identify good practices, nonconformities, gaps and shortcomings; share good practices; offer help in a positive manner; add to lessons learned; reduce CoQ and raise acceptance; confirm approved changes, corrective actions, defect repairs and preventive actions were implemented
Checklists Reminders built from history and lessons learned; never exhaustive; review and update them; also used to confirm readiness ("definition of ready")
Data representation Affinity diagrams, cause-and-effect diagrams, flowcharts (section 7.3)
Problem-solving Define the problem, identify the root cause, generate solutions, choose the best, implement, verify effectiveness
Process improvement / analysis Analyze current processes, find non-value-added steps and constraints, implement better ones; value stream mapping shows steps and time to find waste
Decision-making Voting, multicriteria analysis (Topic 14)

Outputs: quality report (quality issues, recommended corrective actions, summary of QC findings, improvement recommendations), change requests (corrective, preventive, defect repair), and updates to plans and documents. Audit findings that require changing an approved process go through change control.

6Quality Control: Inspect, Test, Measure

QC happens inside Monitor and Control Scope and uses data from the work.

  • Inspection: examination of a work product to determine whether it conforms to documented standards; may be called reviews, peer reviews, audits or walkthroughs; applied to a single activity or the final product; also verifies defect repairs.
  • Testing / product evaluation: an organized investigation to find errors, defects and nonconformance against the requirements. Early testing finds problems sooner and reduces the cost of fixing them.
  • Variance and trend analysis, root cause analysis, performance reviews (Topic 28).
  • Statistical sampling [Beyond PMBOK 8]: test a representative sample rather than every unit when testing is costly or destructive.
  • Results: QC measurements in the format defined in the plan, verified deliverables, quality reports, change requests (defect repair).

6.1 Control charts

  • A control chart shows whether a process is stable and predictable. Control limits (calculated from the process data; usually ±3 standard deviations Beyond PMBOK 8number) differ from specification limits (from requirements).
  • Special-cause signals: a point outside the control limits; about seven consecutive points on one side of the mean (the rule of seven, Beyond PMBOK 8rule); a run of points trending in one direction. Investigate the assignable cause even if every point is inside the limits.
  • Do not adjust a stable process because of normal variation. A process in control may still fail the specifications, and one inside the specifications may be out of control.
  • Control charts also track cost and schedule variances, volume, or frequency of scope changes to test whether management processes are in control.
  • Beyond PMBOK 8 Normal data: ±1σ about 68%, ±2σ about 95%, ±3σ about 99.7%; a six sigma level is about 3.4 defects per million. (PMBOK 8 names Six Sigma as a continuous-improvement approach but gives no figures.)

7Ongoing Quality Reviews (ECO) and the Basic Tools

7.1 Review continuously

  • Reviews should run throughout each phase, not only at phase gates: defects accumulate between infrequent reviews, and deeper end-of-phase reviews still find them late.
  • Review types: peer reviews, design and code reviews, inspections, test results, phase-gate or quality-gate reviews, quality audits, sprint reviews and retrospectives, and definition-of-done checks in every iteration.
  • Make results visible (quality reports, dashboards), agree actions, and feed findings back into the plan and process.

7.2 Quality in agile work

  • Quality is built in through the definition of done (automated tests, accessibility, security, documentation, compliance) and acceptance criteria on each story.
  • Test inside the iteration (continuous integration, test-first practices Beyond PMBOK 8); a separate testing phase at the end finds defects late and delays release.
  • Compliance checks (for example accessibility) belong in every iteration's DoD, not in a final audit.

7.3 The basic quality tools

Tool Use
Cause-and-effect (fishbone, Ishikawa) Traces an effect to root causes; helps find the main cause
Flowchart (process map) Maps steps, decisions, loops and parallel paths; finds weak handoffs and waste
Checklist / check sheet Reminder list; tallies defects by type
Histogram Distribution of data (discrete data)
Pareto chart Beyond PMBOK 8 Ranks causes by frequency; fix the "vital few" first (80/20 idea)
Scatter diagram Beyond PMBOK 8 Shows correlation between two variables; correlation is not proof of cause
Control chart Stability and special causes (section 6.1)
Affinity diagram Groups ideas or causes into clusters
Root cause analysis Finds the underlying reason for a variance, defect or risk; removing all root causes stops recurrence

8Help Ensure Regulatory Compliance (ECO; detail in Topic 23)

  • Treat regulatory and standards requirements as quality requirements: confirm which apply, classify them, put them into the quality plan and acceptance criteria.
  • Plan verification methods that demonstrate compliance (tests, audits, certifications, evidence), and keep evidence in a controlled, accessible repository (approved artifacts must be easy to find for auditors).
  • Build compliance checks into the DoD of each iteration or each phase's exit criteria; do not leave them to a final audit.
  • Reassess when regulations or standards change; compliance threats are risks until they occur (Topic 21).
  • Audits and inspections confirm compliance; findings lead to corrective actions through change control.

9Manage Cost of Quality and Sustainability (ECO)

Category Examples Type
Prevention Training, documented processes, equipment, time to do it right Cost of conformance
Appraisal Testing, inspections, destructive testing loss, audits Cost of conformance
Internal failure Rework, scrap (found by the project) Cost of nonconformance
External failure Liabilities, warranty work, lost business (found by the customer) Cost of nonconformance
  • Optimal CoQ: invest in prevention and appraisal until extra spending no longer pays off against failure costs. More inspection alone does not fix a process that creates defects; prevention costs less than appraisal and failure.
  • Include CoQ in cost estimates and the budget (Topic 17); track failure costs as an indicator that quality planning is weak.
  • Sustainability: sustainability is one of the quality dimensions (Topic 02). Poor quality wastes materials, energy and travel, so prevention reduces environmental cost too. Put sustainability criteria (for example emissions, energy or water use, recycled content, supplier standards) into quality requirements and the DoD, and measure them with metrics (Topic 07).

10Implement Continuous Improvement (ECO; detail in Topic 31)

  • PMBOK 8 names: plan-do-check-act (PDCA), Lean, Total Quality Management, Six Sigma and the Five Focusing Steps (theory of constraints); Kaizen (continual improvement) appears among these ideas.
  • PDCA: plan the change, do it on a small scale, check the results against the target, act (standardize if it worked, otherwise adjust and repeat).
  • Standardize what works: consolidate best practices into a standard checklist or process and update OPAs (Topic 31).
  • Retrospectives and sprint reviews are the team-level engine: commit to a few improvements and put them into the next backlog; track them to completion. Inspect and adapt the improvement process itself.
  • Sources of ideas: audits, process analysis, root cause analysis, lessons learned, benchmarking, stakeholder feedback.
  • Value stream mapping (Lean): show the critical steps and time in each to find waste and improve flow.

11Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Quality planning Quality management plan up front; metrics, audits, test plan Acceptance criteria, definition of done, working agreements Plan for fixed or regulated parts; DoD for iterative parts
QA Formal audits and process reviews Formal or informal; retrospectives and reviews Both
QC Inspections and tests at defined points; phase exit criteria Continuous testing inside each iteration; automated tests Both
Reviews Ongoing peer reviews plus gate reviews Sprint reviews, demos with feedback time Gates for the envelope, sprint reviews inside
"Done" Acceptance criteria met and accepted DoD met for every item Both
Improvement Lessons learned at gates and closure; update OPAs Retrospective every iteration Both
Beyond PMBOK 8 Test-first, continuous integration, definition of ready

12Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor by criticality (safety or high-risk products need more rigor), regulation, product type and technology, team skills, supplier involvement and organizational culture. Industries that rely heavily on design phases (pharmaceutical, construction) invest early to avoid costly late changes (Topic 15).
  • Process automation and AI can speed tests, scheduling and defect analysis; the project manager validates the output (Topic 08).
  • Interactions: quality is part of scope (functional and nonfunctional requirements); quality activities and rework affect schedule; CoQ affects budget; quality risks go in the risk register; supplier quality and audits are part of procurement; stakeholder satisfaction is the ultimate check.
  • How to tell quality management works: deliverables are accepted and stakeholders are satisfied; defect and rework rates fall; audit findings decline and are closed; compliance evidence is complete; the DoD is met every iteration.

13Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. QA is process; QC is product. An audit of procedures is QA; inspection and testing of deliverables is QC.
  2. Prevention beats inspection. When defects keep occurring, invest in prevention and fix the process; do not simply add inspections.
  3. Build quality in: put tests, accessibility and compliance in the definition of done; test early, not at the end.
  4. Reviews are ongoing, not only at phase gates.
  5. Rule of seven: seven consecutive points on one side of the mean (or a clear trend) signals a special cause even inside the control limits; investigate. Do not widen limits or tamper with a stable process.
  6. Control limits are not specification limits.
  7. A compliance or standards requirement is a quality requirement: plan how compliance will be verified and evidenced.
  8. Customer-required sustainability criteria belong in the quality requirements and controls.
  9. Verified is not accepted: QC passes, then the customer validates (Topic 15).
  10. Find the root cause before fixing, then verify the fix worked; use Pareto to start with the vital few.
  11. Grade is not quality: a lower grade can be right; failing the requirements is not.
  12. Quality needs measurable metrics and defined ways to verify them.
  13. Audits are structured, independent and constructive; cooperate, share good practices and act on findings through change control.
  14. Improve the improvement process: commit to a few actions in the backlog; retrospectives that only list ideas do not improve anything.
  15. Standardize what works (update OPAs, checklists) after a successful pilot.
  16. Do not gold-plate: meet the requirements; extra features are not quality (Topic 15).
  17. Quality problems found create change requests (corrective, preventive, defect repair); use change control.

14Exam Q&A

14.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1An independent internal team reviews whether the project is following its documented procedures and standards, and reports gaps in how work is done. Which activity is this?

  • AValidation, because it confirms that the customer accepts the delivered results
  • BQuality control, because it verifies that finished deliverables meet their specifications
  • CContinuous improvement, because it changes the standards of the whole organization
  • DQuality assurance, because it examines the processes rather than the deliverables
Show the answer

Answer: D. Auditing whether activities comply with policies and procedures is quality assurance, which is process-focused and preventive. Quality control inspects and tests deliverables, validation is customer acceptance, and improvement is a separate activity that may follow.

S2An audit finds that a sprint team skips a peer-review step required by the approved process because it slows delivery, and the team proposes to drop the step for good. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk the auditors to withdraw the finding now that the team has explained itself
  • BRaise a change request so the step is reviewed and formally changed if justified
  • CInsist on the step without any discussion, because audit findings are final
  • DAllow the team to drop the step, since the working process belongs to the team
Show the answer

Answer: B. Findings that require changing an approved process go through change control, so the proposal is assessed and, if justified, formally approved. Quietly dropping the step, rigid enforcement or asking auditors to withdraw the finding bypasses that route.

S3A control chart shows a stable, predictable process whose average output lies outside the customer's specification limits. What does this indicate?

  • AThe process is in control but not meeting requirements, so the process itself must change
  • BThe process is acceptable, because points inside the control limits require no action
  • CThe control limits are wrong and should be widened to include the specifications
  • DThe operators should adjust the process after every point that is off target
Show the answer

Answer: A. Control limits come from the process's own data and specification limits from the requirements, so a process can be stable yet fail the specification. The fix is to improve the process, not to widen the limits or tamper with normal variation.

S4A team's defect log lists twelve causes, but two of them account for most of the defects found in the last six sprints. Which tool and approach fit best?

  • AA control chart, then wait until a point falls outside the control limits
  • BA Pareto chart, then tackle the vital few causes first
  • CA histogram, then address every cause equally so that the team stays unbiased
  • DA scatter diagram, then fix the causes in the order in which they were logged
Show the answer

Answer: B. A Pareto chart ranks causes by frequency so the vital few can be fixed first, which is where the largest gain lies. A scatter diagram shows correlation, a histogram shows a distribution and a control chart tests stability, and none of them prioritizes causes.

S5Each crash barrier must be tested to destruction, so testing every unit would leave nothing to sell. How should the project manager plan the testing?

  • ASkip testing and rely on the supplier's certificate of conformity
  • BTest only the units that the customer will inspect on delivery day
  • CTest a statistically representative sample of the units
  • DTest every unit and accept the loss as part of the cost of quality
Show the answer

Answer: C. Statistical sampling tests a representative sample when testing is costly or destructive. Testing only what the customer inspects, relying on a certificate alone or testing everything does not give reliable quality evidence at an acceptable cost.

S6The product team's quality plan states that the mobile app must be "very reliable". What would make this a usable quality metric?

  • AA promise by the team to fix every crash as soon as it has been reported
  • BA customer survey question asking whether the app feels reliable to use
  • CA statement from the sponsor confirming that reliability is important to the business
  • DA measurable threshold, such as fewer than two crashes per 1,000 sessions
Show the answer

Answer: D. A quality metric describes an attribute and how compliance will be verified, so it needs a measurable threshold and a way to measure it. An endorsement, a promise to fix or a feeling in a survey does not define a testable standard.

S7A client orders the basic version of a product with few features and then complains about its quality, although it meets every requirement for that version. How should the project manager respond?

  • AAgree that fewer features means lower quality and offer a price discount
  • BAsk the client to accept the product because the contract is already signed
  • CExplain that low grade is not low quality if the requirements are met
  • DUpgrade the product to the deluxe version at the project's own expense
Show the answer

Answer: C. Grade is a category of products with the same function but different features, and a basic grade that meets its requirements is not a quality problem. Upgrading free of charge, conceding poor quality or insisting on the contract alone misses the distinction.

S8Repeated measurements of a part's length cluster tightly together, but all of them are 5 mm longer than the true length. How should the measurement process be described?

  • APrecise but not accurate, so the measuring equipment should be calibrated
  • BNeither precise nor accurate, because the readings do not vary at random
  • CAccurate but not precise, so more measurements should be taken to average out
  • DBoth precise and accurate, because the readings are consistent with each other
Show the answer

Answer: A. Precision means repeated measurements cluster together, while accuracy means they are close to the true value; these readings are consistent but biased, which points to calibration. The other descriptions mix up the two ideas.

S9After a retrospective, a team restarted a service to stop a recurring production crash, but the crash returned a month later. Which problem-solving step was most likely skipped?

  • ADocumenting the restart in the lessons learned register afterward
  • BDefining the problem, since the crash was clearly observed by everyone involved
  • CGenerating several possible solutions before choosing the best one among them
  • DFinding the root cause and verifying that the fix was effective
Show the answer

Answer: D. Problem-solving defines the problem, finds the root cause, generates and chooses solutions, implements and then verifies effectiveness; a returning crash shows the cause was not found or the fix not verified. The problem was already defined, and documenting afterward would not prevent recurrence.

S10The team fears an upcoming independent quality audit of the hybrid project and asks the project manager to postpone it until the problems are fixed. What should the project manager do?

  • ACancel the audit, since the project already has its own inspection results
  • BAsk the auditors to review only the areas where the team performs well
  • CKeep the audit, cooperate openly and use the findings and shared good practices
  • DPostpone the audit so that the team has time to correct the problems quietly
Show the answer

Answer: C. Audits are structured, independent and constructive: they identify good practices and gaps, and the team cooperates and acts on the findings. Postponing, canceling or narrowing the scope defeats their purpose of building confidence and improving processes.

14.2 Recall Q&As

R1Quality assurance versus quality control in PMBOK 8?

Show the answer

QA uses project processes effectively and follows standards to assure stakeholders; QC creates deliverables that meet defined specifications and thresholds.

R2What does the quality management plan include?

Show the answer

Quality standards, objectives, roles and responsibilities, deliverables and processes subject to review, planned QC and QA activities, tools and methodologies, and procedures for nonconformance and continuous improvement.

R3What is a quality metric? Give examples.

Show the answer

A description of a project or product attribute and how QA verifies compliance with it. Examples: defects per day, failure rate, test coverage, CPI, downtime per month, customer satisfaction score.

R4What are quality audit objectives?

Show the answer

Identify good practices and nonconformities, share good practices, offer positive help, record lessons learned, reduce CoQ, raise acceptance, and confirm approved changes and repairs were implemented. Audits are scheduled or random and usually independent.

R5Name the four cost of quality categories.

Show the answer

Prevention, appraisal (conformance); internal failure, external failure (nonconformance).

R6Control limits versus specification limits?

Show the answer

Control limits are calculated from process data (commonly ±3σ, a figure beyond PMBOK 8); specification limits are set by requirements.

R7What is the rule of seven?

Show the answer

Seven consecutive points on one side of the mean signal a special cause (shift) to investigate, even within the control limits.

R8What is an inspection?

Show the answer

An examination of a work product to determine conformance to documented standards; also called reviews, peer reviews, audits or walkthroughs; also verifies defect repairs.

R9Why test early?

Show the answer

Early testing finds errors and nonconformance sooner and reduces the cost and effort of fixing them.

R10What are the steps of structured problem-solving?

Show the answer

Define the problem, identify the root cause, generate possible solutions, choose the best, implement it, verify effectiveness.

R11What does PDCA stand for?

Show the answer

Plan, do, check, act: the basic loop of continuous improvement.

R12What else is a cause-and-effect diagram called?

Show the answer

A fishbone or Ishikawa diagram; it breaks the causes of a problem into branches to find the root cause.

R13What is the Pareto principle in quality?** **[Beyond PMBOK 8]

Show the answer

A small number of causes (the vital few) produce most defects (the 80/20 idea); address them first.

R14Grade versus quality; precision versus accuracy?** **[Beyond PMBOK 8]

Show the answer

Grade is a category of features (low grade is acceptable, low quality is not). Precision is repeatability; accuracy is closeness to the true value.

15Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
QA vs QC QA = processes, standards, audits (Manage Quality Assurance); QC = deliverables, specs, testing (inside Monitor and Control Scope)
Quality management plan Standards, objectives, roles, reviews, QC and QA activities, tools, nonconformance and improvement procedures
Quality requirements Tests, certifications, validations; measurable; compliance and customer sustainability criteria included
Quality metrics Attribute plus how QA verifies it (defects per day, test coverage, CPI, satisfaction)
QA tools Audits, checklists, process analysis, root cause analysis, problem-solving, process improvement
QC tools Inspections, testing, control charts, variance and trend analysis, sampling
Audit Structured, independent, constructive; share good practices; findings through change control
Control chart Control limits from data (commonly ±3σ) ≠ specification limits; seven points one side or a trend = investigate Beyond PMBOK 8the ±3σ figure and the rule of seven
Basic tools Fishbone, flowchart, checklist, histogram, Pareto, scatter, control chart, affinity
Ongoing reviews Throughout each phase and iteration; DoD checks; sprint reviews and retrospectives
Compliance Quality requirement; plan verification and evidence; controlled repository
Cost of quality Prevention + appraisal vs internal + external failure; optimal level; prevention is cheapest
Sustainability A quality dimension; criteria in requirements and DoD; fewer defects, less waste
Continuous improvement PDCA, Lean, TQM, Six Sigma, 5FS; retrospectives; standardize what works; update OPAs
Problem-solving Define, root cause, options, choose, implement, verify
Agile quality DoD with tests and compliance; test inside the iteration; no end-stage testing phase
Verified vs accepted QC verifies; the customer validates and accepts
Grade vs quality Low grade acceptable; low quality is not Beyond PMBOK 8
First-action pattern Check requirements and plan, find root cause, prevent rather than inspect, include in DoD, review continuously, standardize, change control
